title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would produce a semantic safety violation when applied. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) with emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring. All archived scoring artifacts record every paired episode as safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared LLM candidate was the only generator sample available to both arms; because every shared candidate passed deterministic validation, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is degenerate. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, statistical mapping to archived analysis artifacts, an artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe device configurations is a central NetOps problem. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows propose executable configuration sequences, but textual fidelity metrics do not capture temporal ordering, device dependency constraints, and invariants required for safe application. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed against device images or simulators and semantically scored—exposes planning and execution faults (ordering violations, transient-service interruptions, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss [1].

A common architectural response is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate if violations are detected [2,3]. Prior work indicates such pipelines can repair many syntactic and some semantic faults, but open questions remain about how often deterministic verifiers materially reduce unsafe outcomes in paired comparisons, especially under distribution shift and adversarial prompts [2,4].

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to measure a precisely defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline), under shared_initial_candidate semantics that produce exactly one initial generator output per task to be used by both arms. This semantics constrains the causal contrast: differences between arms can only arise if the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation and the guarded arm applies a repair. Our contributions are (1) a preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation executed to completion; (2) a traceable mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact numeric results; and (3) an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome and targeted recommendations for future GVR experiments that can produce informative contrasts.
sections.related_work:
Executable NetOps benchmarks and emulation frameworks have been developed to evaluate agentic behavior in closed loop rather than only judging textual output [1]. Work on automatic configuration and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that deterministic validators can enable high repair coverage for many classes of faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize tool‑augmented agent architectures, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as necessary for operational trustworthiness in agentic NetOps workflows [3,5]. Engineering papers on configuration analysis tools (e.g., evolution of Batfish) provide precedent for verifier design and incremental verification strategies [6].

Our study differs in three protocol elements that jointly affect inference: (a) a preregistered paired estimand tied to a concrete emulation‑grounded safety outcome; (b) registered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared generator output per task, reused across arms); and (c) deterministic, emulator‑based final scoring. These choices make the causal meaning of the paired contrast explicit: the guarded pipeline can only improve outcomes relative to baseline when deterministic validation of the shared candidate fails and a repair is invoked.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and defined the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) computed on paired tasks. The analysis executor was specified to compute the paired contingency table, a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for discordant pairs. The preregistration and analysis parameters (resamples, seed) are archived in the execution bundle; these archived artifacts are the authoritative trace for numeric outputs.

Design and sampling: The design was paired with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: for each of N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and reused by both arms. Task composition was in‑distribution = 144 (60%), distribution‑shift = 48 (20%), adversarial‑prompt = 48 (20%). Tasks were generated deterministically from a canonical task generator and encoded constraints (initial state, required sequences, preserved fields) to exercise ordering and dependency reasoning under realistic, instrumented difficulty levels.

Model, adapter, and verifier contract: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and an adapter implementing the GVR contract: baseline = interpret-and-score the shared initial candidate; guarded = run deterministic validation on the shared candidate and, if validation fails, permit up to one validator‑triggered repair invocation to produce a repaired final candidate. The deterministic verifier encodes semantic invariant checks relevant to the task family (ordering, resource protection, minimum‑up constraints); verifier PASS/MISS semantics determine whether a repair opportunity is triggered. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the only route for the guarded arm to produce a different final configuration than baseline is (a) the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation and (b) the guarded arm applies a repair within the allowed budget.

Scoring policy, exclusions, and missingness: Final outcomes were binary: unsafe_apply (semantic safety violation would occur on application) vs safe_apply. The preregistration defined clear exclusion rules (e.g., exclude pairs flagged as verifier PASS but emulator unsafe_apply in primary analysis; include them in sensitivity analyses). A retry policy for infrastructure failures allowed up to two retrials; unrecoverable infra failures would be reported and handled per preregistration. All execution, scoring, and missingness counts were recorded in the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240. Exactly one initial generation was produced per task in accordance with shared_initial_candidate semantics; total hosted model calls consumed = 240. No infrastructure failures or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and inference: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline safe_count = 240/240; guarded safe_count = 240/240. The paired contingency table is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe) = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The estimated paired difference (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples and a fixed seed = 1729 is [0.00, 0.00]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numeric outputs are produced by the preregistered analysis executor and are traceable to the archived analysis artifacts.

Validator and repair activity: Across all guarded episodes no validator‑triggered repair was applied: the shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation in every case. Because repairs were never invoked, the guarded final configurations matched the shared initial candidates and therefore matched baseline outcomes for every task and subgroup (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial). Planned sensitivity channels for 'possible false‑safe' flags or infra failures were unused because no such events occurred.

Subgroup behavior: The subgroup slices (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial) are degenerate in this run: all slices show zero unsafe applies for both arms. Consequently no per‑subgroup discordant evidence is available to estimate heterogeneous verifier benefit.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: The registered shared_initial_candidate semantics made generator variability identical across arms by design: both arms received the same single generator sample per task. Under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only diverge from baseline by applying a validator‑triggered repair when the shared initial candidate failed deterministic checks. In this execution every shared candidate passed the deterministic verifier, so no repairs were invoked and no discordant pairs were created. The degenerate contingency (all pairs concordant safe) is therefore a mechanistic outcome of the combined design choices (shared initial generation + verifier coverage) rather than evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary.

Design tradeoffs and operational implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budget and produce tightly paired generator exposures, which can be desirable for some comparisons, but they also make the measured causal effect contingent on initial candidate failures. To make a paired experiment informative about verifier benefit one must (A) allow independent initial draws per arm (thereby measuring an average effect of integrating validation/repair across generator variability), (B) intensify adversarial perturbations or injection strategies so that initial candidates fail validation with nontrivial probability, or (C) expand repair budgets and repair strategies so that repairs can be exercised when validation does detect faults. These alternative designs change the estimand and must be preregistered.

Threats to validity and limitations: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract constrains causal interpretation as explained above. Construct validity: the deterministic verifier encodes a finite rule set and may not cover every semantic fault class; cross‑checks between verifier PASS and emulator outcomes are valuable guardrails for false‑safe detection. External validity: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; extrapolation to heterogeneous production networks requires further validation. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 precludes detecting verifier benefit under this specific paired estimand and settings.

Recommendations for future GVR evaluations: (1) Carefully select generation semantics to align the estimand with the causal question—if verifier causal effect is the goal, permit independent initial generations per arm or inject generator perturbations. (2) Increase repair budget and diversify repair strategies to study repair efficacy and search‑behavior. (3) Strengthen adversary protocols (adaptive adversaries) to reliably exercise verifier failure modes. (4) Enhance verifier semantic coverage and instrument automated checks to detect verifier PASS vs emulator outcome mismatches.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. The empirical outcome under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics was degenerate: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The null paired contrast is explained by the registered semantics and runtime traces: a single shared LLM candidate was produced per task and that candidate passed deterministic validation in every task, so no guarded repairs were invoked. This artifact‑grounded result does not imply verifiers are unnecessary; rather it demonstrates how design choices (generation semantics, adversary strength, repair budget, and verifier coverage) determine whether a paired estimator can be informative. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future experiments that seek to measure verifier benefit under nondegenerate paired contrasts.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. The registered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs) form the authoritative record for numeric results and are included in the submission bundle.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: only the declared model gpt-5-mini was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompting strategies, or temperature settings.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design produced one shared generator sample per task, preventing generator variability between arms and making verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered fixed protocol and do not represent unconstrained adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of checks; undetected semantic fault classes and potential verifier PASS vs emulator outcome mismatches remain possible.
